sermon:
## Running From the God Who Sent You
*Jonah 1: the prophet, the storm, and the pagans who feared the LORD first*

**Text:** Jonah 1:1-17 · **Supporting:** Psalm 139:7-10 · Proverbs 1:24-26 · Romans 1:18-19 · Matthew 12:41

God tells a prophet to go east, and the prophet buys a ticket west. That is the whole book in one sentence. We have read this story as a children's tale about a man and a fish, and we have missed that it is a story about a believer who heard the word of the LORD clearly and decided he would rather drown than obey it. Not a skeptic. Not a pagan. A prophet. The man who knew God best ran from Him hardest.

**The word came, and the prophet went the other way**

"Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me.' But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD" (Jonah 1:1-3). The text gives no hesitation, no argument, no scene of the prophet wrestling in prayer. The word comes and the man moves, but he moves in the exact opposite direction. Nineveh lay to the east. Tarshish was the far western edge of the known world, the last dot on the map. Jonah did not just disobey. He ran for the horizon.

We want a reason, and chapter four will finally give us one. Jonah ran because he was afraid God might forgive Nineveh, and he wanted Nineveh dead. Hold that. The prophet's disobedience was not weakness of nerve. It was strength of hatred. He understood his God well enough to know that a God who sends a warning is a God preparing to show mercy, and he could not stand the thought of that mercy landing on those people. Nineveh was Assyria's capital, the most violent empire of the age, a city that flayed its captives and stacked their skulls. Jonah was not a coward. He was a patriot, and his theology had become a weapon against his enemies.

The text says he fled "from the presence of the LORD," twice in one verse. Every Israelite reading those words knew they were impossible. "Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there. If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there" (Psalm 139:7-8). Jonah had sung that psalm. He believed it. And he bought the ticket anyway. That is the strange arithmetic of the running heart — it knows God is everywhere and runs regardless, because the goal was never to escape God's reach. The goal was to escape God's assignment.

**The storm chased the one man on the boat who deserved it**

"But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up" (Jonah 1:4). The verb is violent. God threw the storm the way a man throws a spear. And here the irony turns sharp enough to cut. The pagan sailors — men who worshiped whatever god the weather seemed to demand — "were afraid, and each cried out to his god" (1:5). They prayed. They threw cargo overboard. They did everything a person does when heaven goes dark. And where was the prophet of the living God? "But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep" (1:5).

Watch the direction of his every movement. Down to Joppa. Down into the ship. Down into sleep. Soon down into the sea, and then down into the deep where "the weeds were wrapped about my head at the roots of the mountains" (2:5-6). Sin has a gravity. It is always a descent, and the descending man is always certain he is in control of it.

The captain wakes him with a sentence that should have broken him: "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god" (1:6). A pagan sea captain has to tell the prophet of Israel to pray. Then the sailors cast lots, and the lot falls on Jonah, and they interrogate him, and Jonah finally says the truest words he has spoken: "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land" (1:9). He fears the LORD. He says it out loud, to pagans, in the middle of running from the LORD. The confession and the rebellion sit in the same mouth. That is not Jonah's problem alone. We confess on Sunday the God we are fleeing on Tuesday. We sing that He made the sea and the dry land, and then we live as though some corner of our life were outside His jurisdiction. I have preached the sovereignty of God from a pulpit on a morning I was steering my own week as if He could not see it. The gap between Jonah's creed and Jonah's feet is the gap I keep finding in myself.

**The mercy was hidden in the swallowing**

The sailors do not want to throw him over. These pagans show more compassion for one fleeing prophet than the prophet will show for a hundred and twenty thousand Ninevites. "They rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not" (1:13). Only when there is no other way do they take Jonah at his word and lift him over the rail, and the sea goes still, and "the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows" (1:16). The first converts in the book of Jonah are pagans Jonah never meant to reach. Mercy is already leaking out the sides of his rebellion.

Then the verse we have turned into a punchline: "And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights" (1:17). The fish is not the judgment. The fish is the rescue. The judgment was the water closing over his head. God appointed the fish the way He appoints everything in this book — the wind, the lot, the plant, the worm — to chase a running man back toward grace he did not want.

Centuries later a greater prophet stood among people demanding a sign, and He pointed back to this chapter: "For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). But here is what Jonah could never have seen from inside the fish. Jonah was swallowed because he ran from his enemies. Christ was swallowed by death because He ran toward His. Jonah went down into the deep against his will, to save a boat he was endangering. Christ went down into the grave by His own choosing, to save the very people who put Him there. The sign of Jonah is not finally about a fish. It is about a God who goes down into the dark after the people His prophet wanted dead.

You cannot outrun your call.

## The Prayer at the Bottom
*Jonah 2: a borrowed psalm from a man who has not yet changed his mind*

**Text:** Jonah 2:1-10 · **Supporting:** Psalm 42:7 · Psalm 31:22 · Psalm 3:8 · Luke 18:13

There is a place beneath the water where a man finally prays. Jonah found it. He had slept through a storm that terrified pagans, but he could not sleep at the bottom of the sea with the weeds wrapped around his head, and so from inside a fish, in the dark, he opened his mouth. This is the chapter we admire most and understand least. We read it as Jonah's conversion. It is not. It is Jonah's rescue, and a rescued man is not always a changed man. The most important sentence in the book is spoken here, and the man who says it has not yet let it touch the one place it needs to reach.

**He prayed from the place he never thought he'd reach**

"Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish, saying, 'I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice'" (Jonah 2:1-2). Notice where he prays from. Not from the deck when the storm rose. Not from Joppa when the word first came. He prays from the belly of Sheol, from the place of the dead, from the bottom of his own rebellion. It took the absolute floor to get the prophet on his knees. Some of us will not pray until we are drowning, and God in His mercy will let the water rise that far, because He would rather have us crying out from the deep than asleep in the hold.

The prayer is almost entirely quotation. Jonah is not composing. He is remembering. "All your waves and your billows passed over me" — that is Psalm 42:7. "I am driven away from your sight" — that is Psalm 31:22. Line after line is stitched from the Psalter he had memorized as a boy. There is something tender in this and something troubling. The tender part is that the word of God hidden in him in the daylight came back to him in the dark. He had nothing of his own to say, so the Scriptures said it for him. That is what they are for. Store them now, because the day will come when you are too far under to find your own words, and the only prayer you will have is the one that was put in you years before.

**He confessed everything except the one thing**

But read the prayer for what it does not contain. There is no repentance in it. Not one word. Jonah recounts his trouble, the water, the weeds, the deep, the gates of the land closing behind him forever. He rehearses his rescue. He vows to sacrifice. But he never says he was wrong to run, and he never mentions Nineveh, and he never asks God to change his heart toward the people he was sent to save. The prayer is all gratitude for his own deliverance and silence about everyone else's. He is glad to be saved. He has not begun to wonder whether anyone else should be.

This is the most honest thing the book does to us, and it is easy to miss because the language is so beautiful. A man can pray the right words from the bottom of the sea and still be holding the same hatred he carried onto the boat. He can quote the Psalms perfectly and have a heart that has not moved an inch toward his enemy. I know this prayer because I have prayed it. I have thanked God for rescuing me on a morning I had no intention of forgiving the person I blamed. The vocabulary of grace and the refusal of grace can live in the same prayer, and the man praying it cannot always tell the difference. Jonah could not.

"When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple" (Jonah 2:7). It is a true sentence. It is also a small one. His prayer reaches the temple; it has not yet reached Nineveh. He wants God's mercy for himself and the closed fist for everyone else, and he does not yet feel the contradiction, because we almost never do. The mercy we receive feels like justice. The mercy God shows our enemies feels like a scandal. Same mercy. Different address. The whole rest of the book is God trying to march Jonah the few feet from his own rescue to someone else's.

**The one true sentence, spoken too soon to be believed**

And then, at the bottom of the sea, the prophet says the truest thing in the book: "Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love. But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD" (Jonah 2:8-9). Salvation belongs to the LORD. It is the theological center of the entire book, and it is the sentence that will eventually destroy Jonah's whole position, because if salvation belongs to the LORD, then it does not belong to Jonah. He does not get to decide who receives it. He does not get to fence it around Israel and keep Nineveh on the outside. If salvation belongs to the LORD, then the LORD may spend it on whomever He pleases, and that is precisely what Jonah cannot bear.

He says it without understanding it. He means it as a doxology about his own deliverance, and he does not yet hear it as a verdict on his own bitterness. That is grace — that God lets him say the true thing before he can live it, plants the sentence in his mouth that will one day undo him. The tax collector in the temple could only beat his chest and say, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner" (Luke 18:13), and that man went home justified, because he knew the mercy was not his to ration. Jonah says a grander sentence and goes home still angry, because he thinks it is.

"And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land" (2:10). He is back where he started, on the dry land he tried to leave, with the word about to come a second time. The deliverance is real. The conversion is not finished. It never is, in a single prayer.

Salvation belongs to the LORD.

## Eight Words and a City on Its Knees
*Jonah 3: the worst sermon ever preached, and the greatest revival ever recorded*

**Text:** Jonah 3:1-10 · **Supporting:** Joel 2:13-14 · Jeremiah 18:7-8 · Ezekiel 33:11 · Luke 11:32

The most successful sermon in the Bible was preached by a man who wanted it to fail. Jonah walks into the greatest city of the ancient world, says eight words with no gospel in them, no invitation, no plea, and the entire city falls on its face from the king to the cattle. It is the largest recorded repentance in all of Scripture, and it was delivered by a preacher hoping nobody would listen. This chapter is glorious and it is dangerous, because it forces a question every preacher and every parent and every believer eventually has to face. What do you do when God blesses people you were hoping He would judge?

**The word came a second time, to a man who had not changed**

"Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, saying, 'Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you'" (Jonah 3:1-2). The second time. There is a whole theology of grace in those two words. God does not retire Jonah for running. He does not raise up a more willing prophet. He comes back to the same man with the same assignment, because the God of this book is relentless with the people He calls, and He will say the thing again, and again, until we go. "And Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD" (3:3). He went. The text does not say his heart had moved. Chapter four will prove it had not. He obeyed God while still hating the errand. Sometimes obedience precedes the change of heart, and a man does the right thing with the wrong soul, and God uses it anyway.

The city was vast — "three days' journey in breadth" (3:3). And Jonah's sermon was the shortest in recorded history. "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown" (3:4). Five words in Hebrew, eight in ours. No mention of the LORD by name. No call to repent. No promise of mercy if they turn. No path offered. Read against any sermon Jeremiah or Isaiah ever preached, it is a non-sermon, a bare announcement of doom, and you can hear in its brevity a man doing the minimum, walking one day into a three-day city and calling it done. He preached judgment and offered no door. He may well have hoped they would not find one.

**The city did what Israel never would**

And then the impossible. "And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them" (Jonah 3:5). They believed God. Not Jonah — God. A pagan empire, with no covenant, no prophets, no Scriptures, no history with the LORD, hears eight grim words from a foreign stranger and turns. The word reaches the throne. "Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything; let them not feed or drink water, but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands" (3:7-8). The king names the sin precisely — the violence in their hands, the thing Assyria was infamous for. Even the animals are draped in sackcloth. The whole creation of that city groans toward repentance.

Here is the indictment buried in the comedy. The prophets spent centuries preaching to Israel — Amos, Hosea, Isaiah, Jeremiah — with signs and wonders and the full weight of the covenant, and Israel would not turn. Jonah preaches eight words with a sullen heart to people who never asked for him, and they repent in a day. Jesus said it to His own generation: "The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here" (Luke 11:32). The pagans who repented at a bad sermon will stand in judgment over the religious who would not repent at a perfect one. That is not a comfortable thing for the people who own the Bibles. It is meant not to be.

**The God who relents, and the prophet who can't forgive Him for it**

Watch what the king hopes for, and watch how carefully he says it. "Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish" (Jonah 3:9). He does not presume. He throws himself on a mercy he has no claim to. And the chapter ends with the sentence the whole book was built to deliver: "When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it" (3:10).

This is exactly the God Israel had always known and Jonah had always feared. "Return to the LORD your God, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love; and he relents over disaster" (Joel 2:13). The LORD had said it through Jeremiah — if a nation turns from its evil, "I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (Jeremiah 18:8). And through Ezekiel — "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). Jonah's whole crisis is that he believes every word of this and hates that it is true when the disaster headed for the city of his enemies.

And I have to ask whether I am Jonah more often than I confess. There are people I would rather God deal with than save. There are names I would not want to see at the front of the church on a Sunday morning, repentant, forgiven, sitting two rows up as if their past had been wiped clean. I have preached a gospel of grace for all and quietly hoped it would skip a few. That is the heart this chapter exposes, and it is closer to mine than I want it to be. The scandal of Nineveh is not that they were too evil to save. The scandal is that I have a list of who grace is for, and God keeps crossing names off it that I had underlined. There is a greater Jonah here — one who did not preach doom to His enemies and hope they'd miss the door, but who hung between heaven and earth and prayed, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." He is the prophet Nineveh's prophet refused to be.

God relents toward His enemies.

## The Question God Left Hanging
*Jonah 4: a withered plant, a furious prophet, and an ending with no last line*

**Text:** Jonah 4:1-11 · **Supporting:** Exodus 34:6-7 · Luke 15:28-30 · Matthew 5:43-45 · Romans 5:8

The book of Jonah ends with a question mark, and God never answers it. After the storm and the fish and the impossible revival, the story does not close with a triumph. It closes with a sulking prophet on a hillside, a dead plant, and a question from God left hanging in the air with no reply written down. That silence is not an accident. The author put down his pen mid-conversation on purpose, because the question was never really for Jonah. It was for whoever picked up the scroll. It is for you.

**He was angry that God was good**

Chapter three ended with the greatest revival in history. Chapter four opens like this: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (Jonah 4:1). The salvation of a hundred and twenty thousand people made the prophet furious. And now, finally, we learn why he ran in the first place. "O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster" (4:2).

He ran because God is good. That is his complaint. And listen to what he is quoting — it is the most beloved description of God in the whole Old Testament, the words the LORD spoke to Moses on the mountain: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love" (Exodus 34:6). Every Israelite treasured that sentence. It was the gospel of the old covenant. And Jonah throws it back in God's face as an accusation. The mercy he loved when it fell on him became intolerable the moment it fell on Nineveh. The very grace that saved him from the deep is the grace he cannot stand to see spent on his enemies. "Therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live" (4:3). He would rather be dead than live in a world where God forgives the people he hates.

**God argues with a plant instead of a sermon**

God does not rebuke him. God asks a question. "Do you do well to be angry?" (Jonah 4:4). And Jonah does not answer. He stomps off, builds a little shelter east of the city, and sits down to watch, still hoping — even now — that the forty days might run out and the fire might fall after all. He wants a front-row seat to a destruction God has already canceled.

So God teaches him with a garden instead of a lecture. "Now the LORD God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant" (4:6). The same verb again — God appointed the plant, as He appointed the fish, the wind, the lot. The prophet who would not rejoice over a saved city rejoices wildly over a leafy shrub. His joy has shrunk to the size of his own comfort. "But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered" (4:7). Then a scorching east wind, and the sun beating on his head, and Jonah back to the only prayer he has left: "It is better for me to die than to live" (4:8).

Now the trap closes, gently and completely. "Do you do well to be angry for the plant?" And Jonah, who has learned nothing, snaps back: "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die" (4:9). He has more compassion for a plant than for a city. He grieves a shrub he did not grow and feels nothing for a hundred thousand souls. And God names it exactly: "You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night" (4:10). The man's whole heart is laid bare in one comparison. He weeps over what costs him nothing and shrugs at what cost God everything.

**The ending He left open on purpose**

And then the last words of the book, and God never gets an answer. "And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?" (Jonah 4:11). That is where it stops. No reply from Jonah. No tidy repentance. No verse telling us he came down off the hill and made peace with the mercy of God. The scroll ends with God's question hanging unanswered, because the author wants you to be the one who answers it.

And I cannot pretend the question is only Jonah's. I have an older brother in me — the one in the parable who stood outside the party furious that the father killed the fattened calf for a son who wasted everything, while the music played and the dancing went on without him (Luke 15:28-30). The elder brother and the runaway prophet are the same man, and he is in the mirror more often than I will admit. We are commanded to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us, "so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, for he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good" (Matthew 5:45). Jonah hated that sun. We hate it too, every time we want grace to be fair, which is to say every time we want it to stop short of the people we have decided do not deserve it.

There is a greater Jonah, and He answers the question Jonah would not. Where Jonah sat above the city wishing it would burn, Christ wept over Jerusalem and longed to gather it like a hen gathers her chicks. Where Jonah went into the deep to escape his enemies, Christ went into the grave to save His. "While we were still enemies, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). We were Nineveh — the violent city, the people who did not know our right hand from our left, the enemies God had every cause to leave to the disaster — and He pitied us. The book of Jonah ends with a question because there is only one true answer, and it is hanging on a cross, with His arms open toward the very people who drove the nails.

Should I not pity them?
